You are black-box characterizing a PyInstaller executable: /workspace/dataset/test12_executable
Its Python source is /workspace/dataset/test12.py (short; you MAY read it). It uses argparse (--a/--b/--c, type=int, all required)
and the `schedule` library, printing job intervals and Job() reprs.

HARD RULES:
- Do NOT extract, unpack, decompile, or run `strings`/binwalk/pyi-archive_viewer on the executable, and do NOT try to read the
  bundled `schedule` package source. Characterize by RUNNING it only. This is a strict black-box exercise.
- ALWAYS wrap every run in `timeout 8` (some inputs loop forever / for minutes). Never run the executable without a timeout.
  Passing 0 to --a/--b/--c hangs forever; -1 to --a or --b takes ~1min+. Budget accordingly and note timeouts as such.
- Capture stdout and stderr SEPARATELY and record the exit code, e.g.:
    timeout 8 /workspace/dataset/test12_executable --a 5 --b 10 --c 3 >/tmp/o 2>/tmp/e; echo "rc=$?"; echo "--out--"; cat -A /tmp/o; echo "--err--"; cat -A /tmp/e
  Use `cat -A` whenever exact spaces/tabs/newlines matter (report the real characters, not the $ markers, in your answer).
- Report EXACT byte-level text: leading/trailing spaces, blank lines, punctuation.

BASELINE (already established, do not re-derive):
  --a 5 --b 10 --c 3  ->  rc=0, stdout:
5
10
3
Job(interval=1, unit=days, do=<lambda>, args=(), kwargs={})
Job(interval=1, unit=weeks, do=<lambda>, args=(), kwargs={})   (x8 more weeks lines, 9 Job lines total)
12

DIMENSION: exactly which strings argparse's `type=int` accepts / rejects, and the exact rejection message.
Hold --b and --c at valid values (e.g. --b 1 --c 1) and vary --a. Determine acceptance and the parsed value.
Test at minimum: "5", "  5  ", "\t5\n", "+5", "-5", "007", "+007", "1_000", "1_0_0", "1__0", "_1", "1_", "-_1", "0x10", "0b101",
"0o17", "1e3", "1.0", "1.", ".5", "", " ", "5 5", "1,000", "inf", "nan", "None", "true", "5x", "x5", "٥" (U+0665 Arabic-Indic five),
"٥٦", "５" (U+FF15 fullwidth five), "５６", "१२" (Devanagari), "𝟝" (U+1D7DD math double-struck five), "²" (superscript two),
"½", "Ⅴ" (Roman numeral), "5\u00a0" (nbsp), "\u20035" (en-quad + 5), "-0", "+0" (NOTE: 0 hangs — use timeout and report rc=124),
"０" (fullwidth zero, also hangs).
For each: does it parse, to what value (read it off stdout line 1), or what is the exact stderr text?
Report the exact invalid-value message format (quoting style around the value, and how weird characters are shown).
Also: is the message repr()-style (e.g. does '\t5' show as '\t5')? Test that specifically.

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

input.dimension: argparse `type=int` acceptance/rejection for --a/--b/--c in /workspace/dataset/test12_executable (PyInstaller-frozen /workspace/dataset/test12.py), and the exact invalid-value error text
rules: Acceptance is exactly CPython `int(str)` semantics (base 10, no base prefix, Unicode-aware). Nothing argparse-specific is layered on top: argparse just calls `int(value)` and turns any ValueError into its own error. There is no range check, no `>=0` check, and no float fallback.

ACCEPTED grammar: `int(s)` where s = [unicode-whitespace]* [ '+' | '-' ] digit+ ( '_' digit+ )* [unicode-whitespace]* . `digit` is any character with Unicode property Nd (decimal digit), not just ASCII 0-9.

Surrounding whitespace is stripped before parsing, using Python's Unicode whitespace set. Confirmed-stripped characters: space, TAB (U+0009), LF (U+000A), CR (U+000D), VT (U+000B), FF (U+000C), NBSP (U+00A0), U+1680 OGHAM SPACE MARK, U+2000 EN QUAD, U+2003 EM SPACE, U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE. Leading AND trailing both allowed, in any quantity/mixture.
Leading zeros are allowed and ignored: '007' -> 7, '+007' -> 7, '00' -> 0.
A leading ASCII '+' or '-' is allowed. Only ASCII '+'/'-'; U+2212 MINUS SIGN is rejected.

PEP 515 underscores are allowed but only as single separators strictly between digits: '1_000' -> 1000, '1_0_0' -> 100 are accepted; '1__0', '_1', '1_' are rejected. '-_1' never even reaches int() (see gotchas).

Any Nd-category digit works and mixes freely with ASCII digits, all valued positionally: '٥' (Arabic-Indic 5) -> 5, '٥٦' -> 56, '５' (fullwidth 5) -> 5, '５６' -> 56, '१२' (Devanagari 12) -> 12, U+1D7DD (MATHEMATICAL DOUBLE-STRUCK FIVE) -> 5, '1٥' -> 15.
Non-Nd numeric characters are REJECTED even though they have numeric value: '²' (superscript two, No), '½' (vulgar one half, No), 'Ⅵ'/'Ⅴ' (Roman numeral, Nl).

Rejected: base prefixes ('0x10', '0b101', '0o17'), any float syntax ('1e3', '1.0', '1.', '.5'), empty string '', whitespace-only ' ', embedded space '5 5', '+ 5', thousands comma '1,000', 'inf', 'nan', 'None', 'true', '5x', 'x5', zero-width space '​5', and undecodable argv bytes (0xFF).

On rejection: exit code 2, stdout EMPTY, and stderr is exactly two lines:
"usage: test12_executable [-h] --a A --b B --c C\n" followed by "test12_executable: error: argument --a: invalid int value: <REPR>\n" (no trailing blank line). Substitute --b / --c for the corresponding flag; the prog name is the executable's basename `test12_executable`.
Format string for the second line: `{prog}: error: argument {flag}: invalid int value: {value!r}` — i.e. the offending value is rendered with Python `repr()`, NOT wrapped in hand-written quotes.

Consequences of repr(): normally single-quoted ('abc'); if the value contains a single quote but no double quote, repr switches to double quotes ("5'x"); if it contains both, it stays single-quoted and backslash-escapes the single quote ('5\'"x'); a literal backslash is doubled ('5\\x'); TAB shows as \t and LF as \n ('\t5x', 'a\nb'); non-printable code points show as \xNN / \uNNNN (NBSP -> '5\xa0X', ZWSP -> '​5'); undecodable argv bytes show as surrogates (byte 0xFF -> '5\udcff').

PRINTABLE non-ASCII characters are emitted RAW (real UTF-8 bytes), not escaped: '²' prints as the actual '²' character, 'Ⅴ' as 'Ⅴ', '−' as '−'. Only non-printable code points get \x/\u escapes. This is exactly Python's repr()/str.isprintable() split.

On acceptance, stdout line 1 is the decimal `str()` of the parsed int (so '007' prints `7`, '+5' prints `5`, '５' prints `5`, '1_000' prints `1000`), then --b's value, then --c's value, then the 9 Job(...) lines, then `12`. 13 stdout lines total, exit 0.

Value 0 (from any spelling: '0', '-0', '+0', '00', fullwidth '０') parses fine but the program then hangs forever inside schedule; observed rc=124 under `timeout 8` with EMPTY stdout and EMPTY stderr. Negative values also parse fine but hang/run very long ('-5' -> rc=124, empty stdout+stderr under timeout 8). Absence of a usage/error message plus rc=124 is the proof that int() accepted the value.

Very large accepted ints escape argparse but crash schedule with exit code 1 and a traceback on stderr: ~1e12 ('999999999999') -> `OverflowError: date value out of range` at schedule/__init__.py line 731; 1e25 -> `OverflowError: Python int too large to convert to C int` at line 729. 2147483647 and 2147483648 both work fine (rc=0), so the limit is NOT C-int range.

gotchas: The invalid-value message is `repr()`, not quoted-by-hand. That means the quote character is NOT always `'`: a value containing an apostrophe (and no double quote) is rendered with DOUBLE quotes, e.g. `invalid int value: "5'x"`. Any reimplementation that hardcodes `'{}'` will diverge.

repr() splits weird characters two ways by `str.isprintable()`. Non-printable => escaped (`\t`, `\n`, `\xa0`, `​`, `\udcff`, lowercase hex). Printable non-ASCII => emitted RAW as UTF-8 (`²`, `½`, `Ⅴ`, `−`). So '²' is NOT shown as '\xb2' but NBSP IS shown as '\xa0', even though both are U+00Bx-ish Latin-1 range.

`--a -_1` does NOT produce 'invalid int value'. It produces `test12_executable: error: argument --a: expected one argument`. argparse's negative-number heuristic only reclassifies `-` -prefixed tokens as values when they match a number pattern; `-_1` looks like an option, so int() is never called. (`--a -5` DOES work — argparse allows it because the parser defines no numeric-looking option strings.)

`int()` is Unicode-aware in a lopsided way: every Nd digit is accepted and mixes with ASCII (`1٥` -> 15, `１２` -> 12, U+1D7DD -> 5), but numeric characters in categories No/Nl are rejected (`²`, `½`, `Ⅴ`). Do not use 'has a numeric value' as the test.

U+1D7DD (MATHEMATICAL DOUBLE-STRUCK FIVE) is ACCEPTED -> 5. Bash `$'\U0001D7DD'` did not expand in this shell and silently passed the 10-character literal `\U0001D7DD`, yielding a false 'rejected' reading. Always feed astral characters as raw bytes: `"$(printf '\xf0\x9d\x9f\x9d')"`.

Whitespace stripping is broader than ASCII: NBSP (U+00A0), U+1680, U+2000, U+2003, U+3000, plus CR/VT/FF are all stripped. But ZERO WIDTH SPACE (U+200B) is not, and is rejected. NBSP being simultaneously strippable AND \x-escaped in error messages is the most surprising pair of behaviours.

Every zero spelling — '0', '-0', '+0', '00', fullwidth '０' — parses successfully and then hangs forever with completely EMPTY stdout and stderr. rc=124 plus zero bytes on both streams is the only observable signal, and it is indistinguishable from a negative value ('-5' looks identical at 8s). Do not read 'no output' as 'rejected'; a rejection always emits the 2-line usage+error block on stderr with rc=2.
Because argparse errors happen before any print, a rejected run has completely empty stdout — the 13-line schedule output is all-or-nothing.

Accepted-but-huge values bypass argparse and die in schedule with rc=1 and a traceback whose PyInstaller tag `[PYI-<pid>:ERROR]` contains the PID and therefore changes every run. Don't byte-compare that line. Also the traceback frames show no source lines (frozen build strips them).

During one batch run, a fullwidth-zero invocation appeared to leave 7 lines of usage text in the stdout file. Three clean re-runs produced empty stdout/stderr with rc=124, and no orphaned processes were found, so that reading was a harness artifact. If you see unexpected content after a timeout kill, re-run in isolation before believing it.
stdout line 1 is `str(int(value))`, so the accepted form is normalized on the way out: '007' -> `7`, '+5' -> `5`, '1_000' -> `1000`, 'Ｕ+FF15' -> `5`. Never assume the echoed value is the input text.
